title: SYSK Selects: How Lie Detectors Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the classic episode on lie detectors. Josh introduces it as a classic pick. The hosts trace the polygraph from early 1920s Berkeley, where police officer John Larson used a cardio-pneumo-psychograph (invented by William Marston) and Leonard Keeler marketed it, through earlier precursors (Lombroso, Vittorio Binosi, James Mackenzie, the unigraph). They explain the three measurements (respiration via pneumographs, blood pressure/heart rate via a cuff, and galvanic skin response via finger electrodes), the polygraph exam structure (pretest, control, relevant and irrelevant questions, post-test), examiner training and lack of licensing, and criticisms that the results are subjective and prone to false positives and negatives (Gary Ridgeway example). They cover legal admissibility (New Mexico, federal judges), the Employee Polygraph Protection Act, countermeasures, fMRI lie detection, and penile plethysmography. The episode closes with listener mail from Brad with satirical suggestions for the show.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick as a classic episode on lie detectors, followed by banter about the Saturday Night Live 'you lie' skit.

segments.title: Early polygraph history in Berkeley
segments.summary: John Larson, a Berkeley police officer with a PhD, used the cardio-pneumo-psychograph invented by William Marston to investigate a string of thefts at College Hall, UC Berkeley. Suspect Helen Graham confessed after days of questioning. Leonard Keeler later marketed the device as a magic lie detector, and Larson later distanced himself from it.

segments.title: Precursors to the polygraph
segments.summary: Early devices by Cesare Lombroso (blood pressure), Vittorio Binosi (breathing, 1904), and James Mackenzie (term polygraph, 1906) led to the unigraph, which measured respiration. The hosts note that polygraphs measure physiological changes rather than detecting lies directly.

segments.title: How polygraph instruments work
segments.summary: The three main measurements are respiration (pneumograph tubes around chest and abdomen with bellows), cardiovascular activity (blood pressure cuff detecting sound), and galvanic skin response (finger electrodes measuring skin conductivity). Analog ink-pen charts have largely given way to digital transducers.

segments.title: Subjectivity and examiner training
segments.summary: Critics such as the ACLU call polygraph data subjective. Proponents say skilled forensic psychophysiologists can account for nervousness. The hosts describe the estimated 5,000 to 10,000 US examiners and the lack of licensing in many states, plus the training path of an academy requiring a degree or experience, a ten-week course, and 25 reviewed exams.

segments.title: How a polygraph test is conducted
segments.summary: The test begins with an hour-long pretest interview used to profile the subject. Examiners set control questions, such as whether the subject has ever lied, to create a baseline. Relevant questions are compared against control questions in the post-test analysis, and results may be inconclusive.

segments.title: Countermeasures, courts, and error rates
segments.summary: Common countermeasures include sedatives and tacks in the shoe. Polygraph results are generally inadmissible in court, with New Mexico the exception and federal judges deciding case by case. False positives and false negatives are discussed, including the case of Gary Ridgeway, who passed a polygraph before later killings. The federal government is both a major user and a major opponent in court.

segments.title: Employee Polygraph Protection Act and alternatives
segments.summary: The Employee Polygraph Protection Act of the late 1980s bars most private employers from forcing employees to take polygraphs. The hosts then discuss fMRI lie detection as an emerging alternative and penile plethysmography used on sex offenders.

segments.title: Listener mail from Brad
segments.summary: Brad suggests nicknames, a separate memoir podcast, and layered audio tracks. The hosts respond to the satirical suggestions.

segments.title: Outro and calls to action
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners who have access to a polygraph to get in touch and sign off.
